A clean, flat textbook illustration showing the experiment to determine the linear expansivity of a solid. A long metal rod is enclosed in a horizontal cylindrical steam jacket. Steam enters through a tube at the top left and exits through a tube at the bottom right. Two thermometers are inserted into the steam jacket. The left end of the rod is firmly fixed to a rigid block. The right end of the rod touches the spindle of a micrometer screw gauge fixed to the table. White background.

A diagram showing a bimetallic strip. Top panel: The straight bimetallic strip at room temperature, with brass (coloured gold) on top and iron (coloured grey) on the bottom. Middle panel: The strip heated, bending downwards (convex on the brass side) because brass expands more. Bottom panel: A simple fire alarm circuit. The heated strip bends downwards to touch an electrical contact point, completing a circuit connected to a battery and a ringing alarm bell. White background.

A clean, flat textbook illustration of a specific gravity bottle used for liquid expansivity. Left: The bottle completely filled with a liquid at room temperature, with a tiny droplet on top of the stopper. Right: The bottle placed inside a beaker of hot water on a tripod stand over a Bunsen burner, with a thermometer in the water. More liquid is overflowing from the capillary tube in the stopper due to thermal expansion. White background.

Two side-by-side line graphs demonstrating the anomalous expansion of water. Left graph: Volume on the y-axis versus Temperature (°C) on the x-axis. The curve starts at a higher value at 0°C, dips down to a minimum at 4°C, and then rises smoothly as temperature increases. Right graph: Density on the y-axis versus Temperature (°C) on the x-axis. The curve starts at a lower value at 0°C, rises to a peak maximum at 4°C, and then falls smoothly. Labels on axes: "Volume", "Density", "Temperature (°C)", with "4°C" explicitly marked on the x-axis of both graphs at the turning points. White background.
